reference.source: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
clinicalPearls: All pulmonary veins drain into the systemic venous circulation rather than the left atrium, so an atrial-level communication is obligatory for survival
Anatomical types are supracardiac, cardiac, infracardiac and mixed, classified by the site of anomalous drainage
Obstructed drainage, most typical of the infracardiac type, produces a critically cyanotic neonate with severe pulmonary oedema and respiratory distress
Unobstructed drainage presents more insidiously with mild cyanosis, tachypnoea, failure to thrive and heart failure from pulmonary overcirculation
Complete mixing means systemic saturation reflects the balance of pulmonary and systemic venous return across the atrial septum
The obstructed form is a true surgical emergency and is not relieved by prostaglandin, which is reserved for duct-dependent lesions
Repair anastomoses the pulmonary venous confluence to the left atrium, with pulmonary vein stenosis being the main late concern
reference.pathophysiology: In total anomalous pulmonary venous return the pulmonary veins fail to connect to the left atrium and instead drain into the systemic venous system, so oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix within the right atrium. Survival depends on an obligatory right-to-left shunt through a patent foramen ovale or atrial septal defect to fill the left heart and systemic circulation. When the anomalous pathway is obstructed, as often occurs when an infracardiac vein passes through the diaphragm, pulmonary venous pressure rises steeply, causing pulmonary oedema, pulmonary hypertension and profound cyanosis. Unobstructed connections instead deliver a large volume of recirculated blood to the lungs, producing pulmonary overcirculation, right heart volume loading and congestive failure.
additionalDifferentials: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome or pneumonia
Other cyanotic congenital heart disease such as transposition of the great arteries
Partial anomalous pulmonary venous return with large shunt
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography to identify the pulmonary venous confluence, drainage site and obstruction
CT or MR angiography to map the anomalous venous pathway when echo is inconclusive
Chest radiograph showing pulmonary oedema in obstructed disease or a snowman contour in the supracardiac type
Cardiac catheterisation in selected cases to define anatomy and pressures
Arterial blood gas and preductal and postductal saturations to assess cyanosis
redFlags: Severe cyanosis with pulmonary oedema in a neonate indicating obstructed drainage
Rapidly worsening respiratory distress unresponsive to ventilation
Signs of low cardiac output and metabolic acidosis
A restrictive atrial communication limiting left heart filling
reference.prognosis: With timely surgical repair the outlook is good, but obstructed neonatal presentations carry significant early risk, and postoperative pulmonary vein stenosis is a serious complication that can recur and worsen prognosis.
pitfalls: Mistaking obstructed disease for primary lung disease or persistent pulmonary hypertension and delaying surgery
Expecting prostaglandin to help, when the lesion is not duct-dependent and prostaglandin may worsen pulmonary congestion
Overlooking a restrictive atrial septum that critically limits systemic output
Failing to monitor for recurrent pulmonary vein stenosis after repair
references: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
